newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan's polyester fibre firms profits seen down.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan's polyester fibre firms profits seen down.

text.p: Pakistan's polyester fibre sector will hit surplus in 1997 after new plants start production, but profits of fibre companies are seen down because of tough competition, analysts said on Friday.

"What we expect in the coming months is a tough competition between the new and old polyester fibre companies for the market share," said Shoaib Saleem, an analyst at brokerage house BMA Capital Management.

Pakistan's fibre production capacity will increase to 391,500 tonnes this year from 289,500 in 1996 as ICI Pakistan has started producing 63,000 tonnes of polyester annually after the completion of its expansion on Thursday.
Ibrahim Fibre Ltd has already started the first line of production of 35,000 tonnes and is expected to double it to 70,000 tonnes later this month, dealers said.
But the fibre demand for 1997 and 1998 is seen at around 253,000 tonnes and 291,000 tonnes.

Dewan Salman, which has the largest installed capacity of 108,000 tonnes, is likely to face tough competition from Ibrahim Fibre, which is in Pakistan's industrial city of Faisalabad, the BMA review of the sector said.
"About 35 percent of Ibrahim Fibre's production would be absorbed by associated companies which are located in its close vicinity in Faisalabad."
"When we say the synthetic sector is bad, it does not mean losses, but lower profits for 1997/98 (July-June)," said Sameer Kakakhel of Carr Mashriq.

"The rising global demand for textiles has improved local spinners' margins, but the theme of the textile sector's revival has been over-played. It cannot absorb the steep rise in the installed fibre capacity," he said.

"The fibre companies are in the doldrums...in the international market there is a surplus supply of polyester fibre and prices slumped because China has stopped its imports. In Pakistan, however, rates cannot be slashed because the production cost is high," said dealer Hina Akhlaq of KASB & Co.

"Either Pakistani polyester fibre producers would have to lower prices or the production, which would affect profits," she said. "The only way out for Pakistan is to find outlets for exports, which again is not an easy task."
The leading brokerage houses have downgraded the earnings of leading synthetic companies, including Dewan Salman Fibres, because of the competition from the new entrants.
Fibre demand grew by 20 percent in the second half of 1996 because the 1996/97 (July-June) cotton crop had been below the target of 10 million bales.
Government officials estimate cotton production at around 9.2 million in 1996/97 against 9.94 million in 1995/96.
But Carr Mashriq's review of the sector says local polyester staple fibre prices will remain under pressure with increasing regional capacity.
"Our forecast assumes an average price of 68 rupees per kilogram in the first quarter of 1997, and 67 rupees per kilogram in the second quarter."
"On an annual basis, we have assumed improved fibre prices of 75 rupees per kg in 1998, but low capacity utilisation will reduce profits by almost 40 percent," Kakakhel said.
